Antibiotic. These are molecules, usually produced by microorganisms or synthesized chemically, that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth by targeting essential bacterial structures or processes. Antibiotics were discovered accidentally in nineteen twenty-eight when Alexander Fleming observed that mold contamination killed bacteria around it. This discovery revolutionized medicine and transformed bacterial infections from often-fatal to treatable. Today, antibiotic resistance—bacteria evolving immunity through genetic mutation—poses a major public health challenge.

Penicillin was discovered from the mold Penicillium and was the first widely used antibiotic. It works by inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis, causing the cell to burst or lyse. Beta-lactam antibiotics, including penicillins and cephalosporins, share a four-membered lactam ring that binds penicillin-binding proteins in the bacterial cell wall. Aminoglycosides like streptomycin and gentamicin inhibit bacterial ribosomal protein synthesis by binding the thirty-S ribosomal subunit, preventing translation. Tetracyclines block bacterial protein synthesis at the thirty-S ribosome and are broad-spectrum, able to treat many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase four, preventing DNA replication and causing cell death.

The principle of selective toxicity underlies antibiotic action. Antibiotics target bacterial structures or enzymes that humans lack—such as peptidoglycan cell walls and seventy-S ribosomes—or structures that differ significantly in eukaryotes. Antibiotic resistance emerges when bacteria acquire mutations or genes through conjugation, transformation, or transduction that confer resistance, expressed as modified target enzymes, efflux pumps, or degradative enzymes. Common resistance mechanisms include beta-lactamase production, which breaks down beta-lactams, ribosomal mutations that prevent antibiotic binding, and active efflux that pumps antibiotics out of the cell. These mechanisms represent the evolutionary response to antibiotic use and a growing clinical problem.
